decks.title: Unseen Passages: Reading Closely — Part 1
goals: Use a five-step plan to read any unseen passage
Tell factual, descriptive, literary and case-based passages apart and read each well
Read tables and shares correctly in factual passages
Make inferences from clues and name a writer's tone with evidence
Work out word meanings from context and answer 1-mark and 2-mark questions

slides.heading: Unseen Passages: Reading Closely
slides.body_md: CBSE Class 11 English Core, **Reading Skills (26 marks)**. Two unseen passages (10 + 8), note making (5) and summary (3). This part is about the passages; Part 2 covers note making and summary.

rows: two unseen passages (factual, descriptive, literary or case-based)

visual.alt: Table of the reading section of the Class 11 school paper: two unseen passages for ten and eight marks, note making for five marks and a summary for three marks, twenty-six marks in all.
visual.caption: Class 11 has no board exam: this is the school annual examination pattern.

slides.narration: Welcome to reading skills. In the school paper, reading carries twenty-six marks. Two unseen passages carry ten and eight marks, note making carries five and a summary carries three. This first part teaches you how to read an unseen passage closely. The second part teaches note making and summary.

slides.heading: Four kinds of unseen passage
slides.body_md: Passages are new to you, so the **skills** are what you prepare, not the topics.

rows: reports information, often with a table or figures
paints a place, person or scene
tells a story or a moment
gives a real-life situation and asks you to apply ideas
what the case supports and what it does not

visual.alt: Table of four unseen passage types: factual, descriptive, literary and case-based, with what each does and what to watch for.

slides.narration: You will meet four kinds of passage: factual, descriptive, literary and case-based. A factual passage reports information, often with a table. A descriptive passage paints a scene. A literary passage tells a moment of a story. A case-based passage gives a real situation. Different passages, but the same careful reading works for all of them.

slides.heading: A five-step plan for any passage
slides.body_md: Reading the questions first tells you **what to look for**, so your first reading already has a purpose.

visual.alt: Flow of the five-step reading plan: read the questions, skim for the gist, scan for each answer, read those lines closely, then answer and check.
visual.caption: SOYL five-step plan for any unseen passage.

slides.narration: Here is a plan that works every time. First, read the questions so you know what to look for. Second, skim the passage for its main idea. Third, scan for the lines that answer each question. Fourth, read those lines closely. Fifth, write your answers and check them against the passage.

slides.heading: Skimming and scanning

rows: title, opening, closing, first line of each paragraph

visual.alt: Table comparing skimming and scanning by purpose, where the eyes go and what each is used for.

slides.narration: Skimming and scanning are two kinds of fast reading. When you skim, your eyes touch the title, the opening, the ending and the first line of each paragraph to catch the gist. When you scan, you hunt for one target such as a name or a number. Use skimming for main idea questions and scanning for detail questions.

slides.heading: Check: the quickest route to the gist
slides.narration: Your turn. You have thirty seconds to find out what an unseen passage is mainly about. Which way of reading helps the most?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a table with a trap
slides.body_md: *A school reading challenge drew these entries (see the table). A report says: Class 9 was the keenest, because it had the most entrants.* **Is the claim fair?**
bullets: **Read the table:** entrants are 40, 30 and 36; the biggest number is Class 9.
**Read the shares:** 25 per cent, 25 per cent and 40 per cent.
**Compare fairly:** keenness is about the share of each class, not the raw number.
**Verdict:** Class 11 was keenest, with 36 of 90 students.

visual.alt: Table of a reading challenge: Class 9 had forty of one hundred sixty students, twenty-five per cent; Class 10 had thirty of one hundred twenty, twenty-five per cent; Class 11 had thirty-six of ninety, forty per cent.
visual.caption: A reading challenge (illustrative data)

slides.narration: Look at this table from a school reading challenge. The report says Class nine was the keenest, because it had the most entrants. But Class nine is also the biggest class. Compare shares, not raw numbers. Forty of one hundred sixty is twenty-five per cent, while thirty-six of ninety is forty per cent. So Class eleven was the keenest.

slides.heading: Inference: reading between the lines
slides.body_md: An inference is a conclusion the passage **suggests but does not state**. It always rests on a clue.

rows: The shutters came down at noon on a working Tuesday, and distant slogans could be heard.
a strike or procession is taking place
She read the letter twice and then folded it into her bag without a word.
The lamp-post had a fresh coat of paint, but the pavement beneath it was still broken.
repairs were cosmetic rather than real

visual.alt: Table showing inference: what the text says, what we can infer and the clue behind each inference.
visual.caption: An inference is clue plus reasoning, never a wild guess.

slides.narration: An inference is a conclusion that the passage suggests but does not state. Each row of this table pairs what the text says with what we can infer and the clue behind it. Shutters coming down at noon with slogans in the distance suggest a strike. If you cannot point to a clue, you are only guessing.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: an inference question
slides.body_md:
*The shutters came down at noon on a working Tuesday. The pavement vendors packed up too, and from the main road came a faint chant of slogans.*

**Question:** What can be inferred?
bullets: **Inference:** a strike or procession is under way.
**Clue 1:** shops close at noon on a working day.
**Clue 2:** vendors leave, and slogans are heard.
**Not acceptable:** a festival, or a power cut: no clue supports these.

rows: The shutters came down at noon on a working Tuesday, and distant slogans could be heard.
a strike or procession is taking place
She read the letter twice and then folded it into her bag without a word.
The lamp-post had a fresh coat of paint, but the pavement beneath it was still broken.
repairs were cosmetic rather than real

visual.alt: Table showing inference: what the text says, what we can infer and the clue behind each inference.
visual.caption: An inference is clue plus reasoning, never a wild guess.

slides.narration: Here is how to answer an inference question. State the inference: a strike or procession is under way. Then give the clues: shops closing at noon on a working day, vendors leaving and slogans in the distance. Notice what is not acceptable. A festival or a power cut has no clue behind it. An inference must be the most reasonable reading of the evidence.

slides.heading: Check: make an inference
slides.narration: Try one. A boy keeps looking at the clock, taps his pen and stands up twice before the bell rings. What is the most reasonable inference?

slides.heading: Tone: the writer's attitude
slides.body_md: Tone is **how** the writer feels about the subject. Name it precisely and prove it with the writer's words.

rows: praise words; effort and result described warmly
if this goes on, may have to

visual.alt: Table of six tone words with meanings and typical clues: admiring, critical, sarcastic, nostalgic, apprehensive and objective.

slides.narration: Tone is the writer’s attitude to the subject. It may be admiring, critical, sarcastic, nostalgic, apprehensive or objective. You find it in word choice. Praise for something bad shows sarcasm. Fond memories of the past show a nostalgic tone. Figures and neutral verbs show an objective tone. In an exam, choose a precise tone word and back it with a detail.

slides.heading: Check: name the tone
slides.narration: Your turn. A grandmother polishes a lamp her own grandmother once lit and smiles as she remembers festival nights when the whole lane glowed. Which tone word fits?

slides.heading: Vocabulary in context
slides.body_md: You do not need a dictionary. The sentence around an unfamiliar word almost always holds a clue.

rows: a nomad, someone who moves from place to place
unlike or but shows the opposite
Unlike her talkative brother, she was taciturn
examples show what the word covers
cereals such as wheat and barley
the whole sentence points to the meaning
the two sides would not move: an impasse

visual.alt: Table of five context-clue types: definition, synonym, contrast, example and general sense, each with a SOYL example.

slides.narration: Vocabulary questions test whether you can use context. Look for five kinds of clue: a definition placed beside the word, a synonym nearby, a contrast word such as unlike or but, examples that show what the word covers, or the general sense of the whole sentence. Then test your guess by putting the meaning in place of the word.

slides.heading: Check: use the general sense
slides.narration: Try this one. A well was so parched in May that even the frogs had left, and villagers carried water from a river far away. Use the general sense to decide what parched means.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a literary moment
slides.body_md: *Grandfather's radio crackled in the corner, as it had every evening since before Rohan was born. He never listened to it; he only kept it company. When the cricket commentary faded into static, he leaned forward and tuned it again, patiently, like a man coaxing a shy animal.*
bullets: **What it shows about him:** loyalty to an old habit, and gentle patience.
**Device:** a simile, comparing his tuning to coaxing a shy animal.
**Writer's attitude:** affectionate: the details are warm, never mocking.
**Evidence:** *kept it company*, *patiently*.

rows: praise words; effort and result described warmly
if this goes on, may have to

visual.alt: Table of six tone words with meanings and typical clues: admiring, critical, sarcastic, nostalgic, apprehensive and objective.

slides.narration: Now a literary moment. The radio is old, grandfather never listens to it, and yet he tunes it again patiently when it fades. This shows loyalty to an old habit and gentle patience. The comparison to coaxing a shy animal is a simile. The writer’s attitude is affectionate, because every detail is warm. Notice how each point is tied to the words of the passage.

slides.heading: How a case-based set is marked
slides.body_md: The chapter tests use **4-mark case sets**. The school passages of 10 and 8 marks have more parts of the same kinds.

rows: multiple choice, true or false, fill the blank
the one best answer, checked against the passage
two objective parts and a 2-mark answer of about 30 to 50 words
a point with support in own words

visual.alt: Table of two shapes of a four-mark case-based set: four one-mark parts, or two one-mark parts and one two-mark answer, with what earns marks.
visual.caption: Scale up: the school passages of 10 and 8 marks carry more parts of the same kinds.

slides.narration: Here is how a four mark case set is built. Either four one-mark parts, such as multiple choice, true or false and fill the blank, or two one-mark parts and a two-mark answer of about thirty to fifty words. The school passages of ten and eight marks simply carry more parts of these same kinds. Accuracy and relevance earn marks, not length.

slides.heading: Summary: reading unseen passages
bullets: Five steps: questions, skim, scan, read closely, answer and check.
Four passage types: factual, descriptive, literary, case-based.
For tables, compare shares, not raw numbers.
Inference = clue + reasoning; tone = attitude shown by word choice.
Use context clues for vocabulary; two-mark answers: point + support.

visual.alt: Flow of the five-step reading plan: read the questions, skim for the gist, scan for each answer, read those lines closely, then answer and check.
visual.caption: SOYL five-step plan for any unseen passage.

slides.narration: To sum up. Follow the five steps: questions, skim, scan, read closely, answer and check. Know the four kinds of passage. With a table, compare shares, not raw numbers. Base every inference on a clue and name tone precisely. Use context clues for vocabulary. And keep two-mark answers to a point and its support.

slides.heading: Exam tips: unseen passages
bullets: Answer from the passage, not from general knowledge.
Watch for NOT and EXCEPT in questions.
Write units and shares with every figure from a table.
Name tone with a precise word and one detail; avoid good and bad.
Common slips: copying whole sentences; guessing without a clue; one-word answers to 2-mark questions.

rows: title, opening, closing, first line of each paragraph

visual.alt: Table comparing skimming and scanning by purpose, where the eyes go and what each is used for.

slides.narration: Exam tips. Answer only from the passage, even if you know more about the topic. Watch for the words not and except in questions. Write the unit with every figure. Name a tone with a precise word and one detail. And avoid the usual slips: copying whole sentences, guessing without a clue, and one-word answers to two-mark questions.

decks.title: Note Making and Summary — Part 2
goals: Make notes with a title, headings, sub-headings and points
Choose headings that name a whole group of points
Use abbreviations sensibly and explain your own in a key
Write a summary of about 50 words from the main ideas, in your own words
Meet the school marking criteria for notes (5) and summary (3)

slides.heading: Note Making and Summary
slides.body_md: In the school paper, note making carries **5 marks** and the summary **3 marks**. Both start from the same careful reading of a passage; the summary is written from the notes.

rows: title; headings and sub-headings; complete short points; abbreviations with a key
main ideas; brevity near 50 words; own words and correct expression

visual.alt: Table of how note making and summary are marked: five marks for notes for title, headings, short points and key; three marks for summary for main ideas, brevity and expression.
visual.caption: SOYL reading of the school pattern; the chapter tests score the same criteria.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Note making carries five marks and the summary carries three. Both begin with careful reading of the same passage. In fact, the usual route is to make notes first and then write the summary from your notes. This part shows you the method and the marking.

slides.heading: Notes and full text compared
columns:
**Full text**

- complete sentences
- examples, colour, repetition
- meant to be read once, slowly

**Notes**

- short phrases and facts
- headings and sub-headings
- meant to be revised quickly

rows: a smaller group under a heading
every abbreviation explained, at the end

visual.alt: Table of the levels of a set of notes: title, heading, sub-heading, points and key, each with an example and the rule for it.

slides.narration: Full text uses complete sentences, examples and colour. It is made to be read slowly, once. Notes are the opposite. They keep short phrases and facts, grouped under headings, so you can revise quickly. The table shows the levels of a set of notes: a title, headings, sub-headings, points and a key.

slides.heading: Five steps to good notes
slides.body_md: Do the thinking **before** you write: grouping is where most marks are won.

visual.alt: Flow of making notes: skim for the gist, pick the main points, group under headings, shorten and abbreviate, then add a title and a key.
visual.caption: SOYL five steps for notes.

slides.narration: Here are five steps. Skim the passage for its gist. Pick the main points. Group them under headings. Shorten the points and abbreviate where sensible. Finally add a title and a key. Notice that grouping comes before writing. If you know your headings first, the points fall into place.

slides.heading: Choosing headings
slides.body_md: A heading names a **group**; the points beneath it must all belong to that group.

rows: names the group; points are causes
The pollution that is bad for us

visual.alt: Table of four headings with verdicts: causes of pollution is good, pollution is too wide, factory in the town is too narrow and a sentence-like heading is weak.

slides.narration: A good heading names a whole group of points. Causes of pollution is good, because every point under it is a cause. The word pollution alone is too wide. A heading like factory in the town is too narrow, since it names one example. And a long sentence is not a heading at all. Test each heading by asking whether every point beneath it fits.

slides.heading: Check: which heading fits?
slides.narration: Your turn. A passage lists three ways a school can save water: mending leaks, using buckets instead of hoses and collecting rainwater. Which heading covers all three?

slides.heading: Abbreviations and the key
slides.body_md: Abbreviate **points**, never the title. Standard forms need no key; your own forms do.

rows: explain your own forms in the key
+, with a cause arrow in own notes

visual.alt: Table of abbreviation rules: use standard forms, explain your own in a key, abbreviate points and not the title, and stay readable.

slides.narration: Abbreviations save time, but only if the reader understands them. Standard forms, such as govt, e.g. and approx, need no explanation. Your own forms, such as bks for books, must be listed in a key at the end of the notes. Abbreviate points, not the title, and do not shorten every word, or your notes become unreadable.

slides.heading: Check: acceptable abbreviation
slides.narration: Quick check. Which of these abbreviations can be used in notes without an entry in the key?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: notes from a short passage
slides.body_md: *Indian crops fall into two main seasons. Kharif crops such as rice, maize and cotton are sown in June or July, depend on monsoon rain and are harvested in September or October. Rabi crops such as wheat, mustard and gram are sown in October or November, rely on winter irrigation and are harvested in March or April.*
bullets: **Title:** Kharif and Rabi Crops.
**Headings:** 1. Kharif, 2. Rabi.
**Sub-points:** sowing and harvest, crops, water need.
**Key:** irrig. = irrigation.

rows: 1. Kharif: 1.1 sown Jun-Jul, harvest Sep-Oct; 1.2 rice, maize, cotton; 1.3 needs monsoon
2. Rabi: 2.1 sown Oct-Nov, harvest Mar-Apr; 2.2 wheat, mustard, gram; 2.3 needs winter irrig.

visual.alt: A set of model notes on kharif and rabi crops with a title, two headings with sub-points, and a key.

slides.narration: Here is a short passage on kharif and rabi crops. The title sums it up. The two seasons become the two headings. Under each, the same three sub-points appear: when sown and harvested, which crops, and what water they need. Short phrases replace sentences, and the one abbreviation of my own, irrig, is explained in the key.

slides.heading: Check: find the sub-point
slides.narration: Your turn. Notes on cycling have the heading, benefits of cycling. Which of the options belongs beneath it as a sub-point?

slides.heading: Summary: what it is and how to write it
slides.body_md: A summary is the passage **shortened, in your own words**, with the writer's ideas and no one else's.

visual.alt: Table of dos and do nots in summary writing: cover main ideas, use own words, drop examples, write connected sentences and stay near fifty words; do not copy, add opinion, include minor details, use bullets or exceed the limit.

slides.narration: A summary shortens the passage in your own words. It covers every main idea, drops most examples and detail, and is written in connected sentences, not points. Do not copy whole sentences and do not add your own opinion. Aim for about fifty words; the school scheme accepts a little less or a little more.

slides.heading: Five steps to a summary
slides.body_md: Your **notes** are the best starting point: the headings give you the main ideas.

visual.alt: Flow of writing a summary: read and mark the main ideas, cross out examples, join the ideas in your own words, count and trim, and check grammar.
visual.caption: SOYL five steps for a summary.

slides.narration: Here are five steps. Read and mark the main ideas. Cross out the examples. Join the ideas in your own words. Count the words and trim. Finally check grammar and spelling. If you have already made notes, your headings are the main ideas, so the first two steps are nearly done.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: from notes to summary
slides.body_md: Using the notes on kharif and rabi crops:
bullets: **Main ideas:** two seasons; sowing and harvest times; crops; water source.
**Cut:** the individual crop names, apart from one example each.

**Draft:** *Indian crops follow two seasons. Kharif crops such as rice are sown in June or July, watered by monsoon rain and harvested in autumn. Rabi crops such as wheat are sown in October or November, irrigated in winter and harvested in March or April.*
**Count:** about 45 words.

visual.alt: Table comparing kharif and rabi crops by sowing, harvest, crops and water: kharif is sown in June to July and harvested in September to October, rabi is sown in October to November and harvested in March to April.
visual.caption: Indian crop seasons, as used in the worked examples

slides.narration: Now turn the notes into a summary. The main ideas are the two seasons, their sowing and harvest times, a crop for each, and the water source. Most crop names are cut, keeping one example each. The draft joins the ideas in connected sentences and in fresh words. It runs to about forty-five words, inside the limit.

slides.heading: Check: what goes into a summary?
slides.narration: Try this one. A paragraph says tea needs rain, warm weather and hilly slopes, gives Assam as an example and ends with a remark that tea is a favourite drink. A short summary should give priority to which of the options?

slides.heading: Compressing words and figures
slides.body_md: Brevity is a skill: say the same thing in fewer, **stronger** words.

rows: It has been seen that in the last few years
grow crops, rear animals and sell milk

visual.alt: Table of ways to compress wording in a summary: recently for in the last few years, many for a large number, four in five for a ratio, and a single word for a list.

slides.narration: Brevity is a skill. Replace a long phrase with a short one: recently for in the last few years, and many students for a large number of students. Turn a ratio into a fraction a reader can grasp: two thousand four hundred out of three thousand becomes four in five. Replace a list with one word that covers it, as farm covers growing crops and rearing animals.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: trimming a draft
slides.body_md: *Draft:* Many students, about two hundred in all, have been taking part, every Saturday morning, in a clean-up of the lake, which has pleased the council, and which the council has praised in a letter.
bullets: **Keep:** who, what, how often, the result.
**Cut:** the exact number, *in all*, and the letter.
**Trimmed:** *Many students clean the lake every Saturday morning, and the council has praised them.*
**Saved:** about 17 words.

rows: It has been seen that in the last few years
grow crops, rear animals and sell milk

visual.alt: Table of ways to compress wording in a summary: recently for in the last few years, many for a large number, four in five for a ratio, and a single word for a list.

slides.narration: Here is a draft that wastes words. Keep the important parts: who is doing it, what they do, how often, and the result. Cut the exact number, in all, and the letter. The trimmed version says many students clean the lake every Saturday morning, and the council has praised them. That saves about seventeen words and loses no main idea.

slides.heading: How notes and summary are marked

rows: title; headings and sub-headings; complete short points; abbreviations with a key
main ideas; brevity near 50 words; own words and correct expression

visual.alt: Table of how note making and summary are marked: five marks for notes for title, headings, short points and key; three marks for summary for main ideas, brevity and expression.
visual.caption: SOYL reading of the school pattern; the chapter tests score the same criteria.

slides.narration: Notes carry five marks, for a suitable title, logical headings and sub-headings, complete short points and abbreviations with a key. The summary carries three marks, for covering the main ideas, keeping near fifty words and writing in your own correct words. Neither rewards length. Both reward choosing, grouping and compressing.

slides.heading: Summary: notes and summary
bullets: Notes: title, headings, sub-headings, short points, key.
A heading names a whole group; every point must fit it.
Abbreviate points, not the title; explain your own in the key.
Summary: main ideas, own words, about 50 words, no opinion.
Notes first, then summary from the headings.

visual.alt: Flow of making notes: skim for the gist, pick the main points, group under headings, shorten and abbreviate, then add a title and a key.
visual.caption: SOYL five steps for notes.

slides.narration: To sum up. Notes need a title, headings, sub-headings, short points and a key. A heading names a whole group. Abbreviate points, not the title, and explain your own abbreviations. A summary covers the main ideas in your own words in about fifty words, with no opinion. And the best route is notes first, then summary from the headings.

slides.heading: Exam tips: notes and summary
bullets: Spend about 8 to 10 minutes on the notes and 6 to 8 on the summary.
Never write notes as full sentences; do not copy lines from the passage.
Always give a title and a key if you abbreviate.
Count your summary; draft, then trim to about 50 words.
Common slips: opinions in a summary; headings too wide or too narrow; abbreviations with no key.

rows: names the group; points are causes
The pollution that is bad for us

visual.alt: Table of four headings with verdicts: causes of pollution is good, pollution is too wide, factory in the town is too narrow and a sentence-like heading is weak.

slides.narration: Exam tips. Give the notes about eight to ten minutes and the summary about six to eight. Never write notes as full sentences. Always add a title, and add a key if you abbreviate. Count your summary and trim it to about fifty words. The usual slips are opinions in a summary, headings that are too wide or too narrow, and abbreviations with no key.

sections.heading: 1. The reading section at a glance
sections.body_md:
Class 11 has no board exam: the school annual examination carries **26 marks** for reading. Two unseen passages carry **10 + 8** marks, note making **5** and summary **3**.

SOYL chapter tests use the class-default pattern: 4-mark case-based passage sets, 5-mark note-making and reading answers, 3-mark summaries (about 50 words) and objective questions on the conventions.

sections.body_md:
**Five-step plan:** read the questions, skim for the gist, scan for each answer, read those lines closely, answer and check.

**Skimming** looks at the title, opening, ending and first line of each paragraph. **Scanning** hunts for one detail.

**Types:** factual (reports information), descriptive (paints a scene), literary (a story moment), case-based (a real-life situation). Different passages, same plan.

sections.heading: 3. Inference, tone and vocabulary
sections.body_md:
**Inference:** a conclusion the text suggests but does not state; it must rest on a clue.

**Tone:** the writer's attitude shown by word choice: admiring, critical, sarcastic, nostalgic, apprehensive, objective. Name it precisely and prove it with a detail.

**Vocabulary in context:** five clue types (definition, synonym, contrast, example, general sense). Test the meaning by substitution.

**Fact or opinion:** a fact can be checked; an opinion judges or recommends.

key_terms.definition_md: A reasonable conclusion drawn from clues in the text.
The writer's attitude to the subject, shown by word choice.

sections.heading: 4. Reading data and numbers
sections.body_md:
In a factual or case-based passage with a table: read **across** a row for one item, **down** a column to compare. Compare **shares**, not raw numbers, when groups differ in size.

A gap between two percentages is in **percentage points**; a change measured against the start is a per cent change. Two things that happen together do not prove that one **causes** the other.

Always write the unit with a figure.

sections.heading: 5. Note making: layout and headings
sections.body_md:
Notes have **levels**: a **title** that sums up the passage; **headings** that name groups; **sub-headings** for smaller groups; **points** in short phrases; a **key** at the end.

**Steps:** skim, pick main points, group under headings, shorten and abbreviate, add title and key.

A heading must name a **whole group**: not too wide (Pollution), not too narrow (one example), and a label, not a sentence. Use numbering (1, 1.1) or indentation.

sections.heading: 6. Abbreviations and the key
sections.body_md:
Use **standard** abbreviations freely (govt., e.g., esp., approx., w/o, hrs, yr). Your **own** forms (bks, stdts) must be listed in a **key** at the end of the notes.

Abbreviate points, not the title. Symbols such as + or an arrow may be used if they are clear. Do not abbreviate so heavily that the notes cannot be read. A notes answer made of full sentences, or copied lines, loses marks.

sections.heading: 7. Summary writing
sections.body_md:
A summary is a **short account of the main ideas in your own words**, about **50 words** (40 to 60 accepted by SOYL).

**Steps:** mark main ideas, cross out examples, join ideas in your words, count and trim, check grammar.

**Do:** cover every main idea; connected sentences; drop most examples. **Do not:** copy sentences, add opinion, use bullets. Work from your notes: the headings are the main ideas.

**Compress:** *recently* for *in the last few years*; *four in five* for *2,400 of 3,000*.

A point the passage cannot do without, as opposed to an example or a detail.

sections.body_md:
**Objective parts:** choose the one best option; watch NOT and EXCEPT; beware options true in life but not in the passage.

**Two-mark answers (30 to 50 words):** point + support in own words.

**Notes (5):** title, headings and sub-headings, short points, key. **Summary (3):** main ideas, about 50 words, own words.

**Time (a guide):** about 15 to 18 minutes per unseen passage, 8 to 10 for notes, 6 to 8 for the summary.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Marks (school paper):** reading 26 = two unseen passages 10 + 8, note making 5, summary 3. SOYL chapter tests use 4-mark case sets, 2-, 3- and 5-mark constructed answers and 1-mark objective questions.

**How marks are awarded**
- Case parts: the one best answer; 2-mark answers a point plus support from the passage in your own words.
- Notes (5): title 1, headings and sub-headings 2, complete short points 1, abbreviations with a key 1.
- Summary (3): main ideas 1.5, brevity 0.5, expression 1.

**Common mistakes**
1. Answering from general knowledge instead of the passage.
2. Guessing an inference with no clue; vague tone words (*good*, *bad*).
3. Comparing raw numbers when groups differ in size.
4. Notes in full sentences, or headings too wide or too narrow.
5. Abbreviations with no key.
6. A summary that copies sentences or adds an opinion.

**Time:** plan the section so that nothing is left half-done.

ironic, because the writer says the word had lost its meaning for the residents
ironic, because the committee is mentioned
appreciative, because the word patience is positive

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ironic, because the writer says the word had lost its meaning for the residents. start planning again from the beginning
ask the teacher to design the experiment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** start planning again from the beginning. After repeated failure, going back to the drawing board means to rethink the plan from the start.

questions.stem_md: In School P, 45 of 150 students cycle to school; in School Q, 60 of 250 do (illustrative data). A reporter writes that Q is the more cycling-friendly school because it has more cyclists. Which conclusion do the figures support?

options.text_md: Q has the larger share of cyclists because 60 is more than 45.
The two schools have the same share of cyclists.
A larger share of students at School P cycle (30 per cent against 24 per cent), though Q has more cyclists.
The figures say nothing about cycling at either school.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A larger share of students at School P cycle (30 per cent against 24 per cent), though Q has more cyclists. 45 of 150 is 30 per cent and 60 of 250 is 24 per cent. Raw numbers mislead when the groups differ in size; compare shares.

questions.stem_md: A library lent 120 books in January, 150 in February, 180 in March and 144 in April (illustrative data). Between which two consecutive months was the percentage rise largest?

options.text_md: The rise was the same in every pair

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** January to February. January to February: 30 on 120 is 25 per cent. February to March: 30 on 150 is 20 per cent. March to April is a fall. Equal rises in number do not mean equal percentages.

questions.stem_md: Which of these statements is a fact rather than an opinion?

options.text_md: The canteen samosas are the best in the city.
Nobody should ever eat anything else for lunch.
The canteen should be rebuilt at once.
The canteen sold 320 samosas on Friday.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The canteen sold 320 samosas on Friday. A fact can be checked against a record; the others judge or recommend.

questions.stem_md: A passage explains that cyclones form over warm seas, hit the east coast of India more often than the west, and cause fewer deaths today because of early warnings and shelters. Which title suits notes on it best?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Cyclones: Formation, Impact and Safety. A title should sum up the whole passage; the other options name only a place, a cause or a single measure.

questions.stem_md: Which of these abbreviations is unacceptable in notes because no reader could guess its meaning without a key?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** qzv for canal. An abbreviation should be standard or obviously related to the word; a random letter group is neither.

questions.stem_md: In note making, a sub-heading is…

options.text_md: a smaller group of points placed under a main heading
the last line of the notes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a smaller group of points placed under a main heading. Notes work in levels: heading, then sub-heading, then points.

questions.stem_md: A passage says that the canal silted up, so boats could no longer reach the market, so traders moved to the road, and the river port declined as a result. Which set of notes keeps the logic of the passage most faithfully?

options.text_md: Canal; boats; market; traders; road; port
Canal silted → boats cannot reach market → traders shift to road → port declines
Port declined; canal silted; traders on road; boats stopped
Canal, market and port are all important to the town

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Canal silted → boats cannot reach market → traders shift to road → port declines. The passage is a chain of causes and results. Only a version that keeps the links in order preserves it; a bare list or a scrambled order loses the reasoning.

questions.stem_md: Where should the key to the abbreviations you have used be written?

options.text_md: at the end of the notes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** at the end of the notes. The key follows the notes so a reader can look up each abbreviation.

questions.stem_md: Notes under the heading *Causes of road accidents* read: 1.1 over-speeding; 1.2 drunk driving; 1.3 helmets reduce head injuries; 1.4 poor street lighting. Which point is out of place?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 1.3. Helmets reduce injury; they are a remedy or effect, not a cause, so the point belongs under another heading.

questions.stem_md: A summary is…

options.text_md: a copy of the first paragraph
a list of every example in the passage
a short account of the main ideas of a passage in your own words

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a short account of the main ideas of a passage in your own words. A summary shortens without changing the writer's ideas.

questions.stem_md: Read: *Honeybees visit flowers for nectar and, without meaning to, carry pollen from plant to plant, which lets many crops form fruit. In some regions their numbers have fallen because of pesticides, loss of wild flowers and disease. Farmers there now sometimes pollinate by hand, which is slow and costly. Protecting hedgerows and using fewer chemicals are the simplest remedies.* Which is the best summary?

options.text_md: Bees collect nectar from flowers and carry pollen.
Honeybees visit flowers for nectar and carry pollen from plant to plant, which lets many crops form fruit, and in some regions their numbers have fallen.
Bees pollinate many crops, but pesticides, habitat loss and disease have reduced them, so protecting flowering habitat and cutting chemicals is the best remedy.
Farmers are careless with chemicals and should be punished.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Bees pollinate many crops, but pesticides, habitat loss and disease have reduced them, so protecting flowering habitat and cutting chemicals is the best remedy. It is complete (role, decline, causes, remedy), in fresh words and free of opinion. The others are partial, copied or opinionated.

questions.stem_md: A passage tells how a river town cleaned its ghats: a ban on plastic bags, weekend volunteer drives and fines for dumping. It includes a fisherman's joke about the old smell, and ends with the return of fish to the river. A summary of about 50 words should include…

options.text_md: the three actions and the return of the fish
the fisherman's joke and the old smell
only the ban on plastic bags

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the three actions and the return of the fish. Main ideas are the actions and their result; the joke is colour and the names are detail.

questions.stem_md: A passage says that of 3,000 students, 2,400 now use the library every week. Which is the best way to carry this into a summary?

options.text_md: Four in five students now use the library weekly.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Four in five students now use the library weekly. 2,400 out of 3,000 is 80 per cent, which is four in five. A good summary compresses a figure without losing its meaning.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Notes are usually written in short phrases rather than full sentences.

**Reason (R):** Notes are meant to be read quickly and revised later.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Brevity serves quick reading and revision, so the reason explains the practice.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In notes, a sub-heading is placed under a main heading.

**Reason (R):** A sub-heading must always be longer than the main heading.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Sub-headings nest under headings, but no rule makes them longer; length is irrelevant.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A summary may include the summary-writer's own opinion on the topic.

**Reason (R):** A summary reports the ideas of the original writer.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Because a summary reports the writer's ideas, a personal opinion has no place in it.

questions.stem_md:
In March a village library began a weekly story hour. Monthly loans were 30 in March and 90 in June, and the librarian said the story hour had caused the rise.

**Assertion (A):** The figures prove that the story hour caused the rise in loans.

**Reason (R):** Loans tripled between March and June.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The tripling is correct (30 to 90), but two things happening together do not prove cause: other reasons, such as exams or holidays, are possible.

questions.stem_md:
Read: *How thoughtful of the airline to announce the delay only after we had waited four hours at the gate.*

**Assertion (A):** The tone of the sentence is sarcastic.

**Reason (R):** It praises an action which, in the context, was late and unhelpful.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The praise word conflicts with the facts (announcing late), and that conflict is exactly what makes the tone sarcastic.

questions.stem_md:
A town's bus service carried 40,000 riders in 2022 and 46,000 in 2023. In the same period the number of buses rose from 50 to 52.

**Assertion (A):** Ridership rose by a much larger percentage than the number of buses.

**Reason (R):** The number of riders per bus was higher in 2023 than in 2022.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Riders rose by 15 per cent (6,000 on 40,000) and buses by 4 per cent (2 on 50), so A is true. Riders per bus rose from 800 to about 885, so R is true; but R is a result of A, not its explanation.

questions.stem_md: True or false: an abbreviation of your own should be explained in a key at the end of your notes.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Without a key, a reader cannot be sure what a personal abbreviation stands for.

questions.stem_md: True or false: a 50-word summary should keep every example from the passage so that it is complete.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Examples illustrate points; a summary keeps the points and drops most examples.

questions.stem_md: True or false: an inference may rest on the reader's general opinion even when the passage offers no clue.
questions.solution_md: **False.** An inference must be supported by clues in the text; without a clue it is only a guess.

questions.stem_md: A rise from 12 per cent to 18 per cent is a rise of six ___.
questions.solution_md: A gap between two percentages is stated in percentage points.

questions.stem_md: Notes begin with a ___ that sums up the passage and group their points under ___ and sub-headings.
questions.solution_md: A good set of notes has a title, headings and sub-headings, then points.

questions.stem_md: Match each abbreviation used in notes with its meaning.
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). These are standard abbreviations.

questions.stem_md: Match each tone word with the description that fits it.

match_right.text_md: reporting facts without showing personal feeling
worried about what may happen next
saying the opposite of what is meant, in order to mock

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Tone words name the writer's attitude.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of making notes in a sensible order.

options.text_md: Write the key to the abbreviations at the end
Read the passage for its overall idea
Group them under headings and sub-headings
Pick out the main points and sub-points

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (d) → (c) → (a). You must know what the passage says before choosing, grouping and labelling points; the key comes last.

questions.stem_md: At six in the morning Neha's hostel room still had its light on. Her desk was covered with sheets of rough work, and four empty tea mugs stood beside her books. What can you infer about Neha? Give one clue.
questions.solution_md: Inference: she studied through the night. Clues: light on, rough work, tea mugs.

answer.model_answer_md: Neha has probably been studying all night, perhaps for an exam. The light is still on at six, her desk is covered with rough work, and the four mugs of tea suggest that she has been awake for hours, trying to stay alert.

marking_scheme.step: The point or inference that answers the question
Support from the passage, in own words

questions.stem_md: Read: *The minister described the flooded underpass as a temporary inconvenience. Residents, who had waded through chest-deep water for four days, were less relaxed about it.* Is the writer's attitude to the minister's description critical or approving? Support your answer with one detail.
questions.solution_md: Judgement: critical. Support: the contrast between a mild phrase and four days in deep water.

answer.model_answer_md: Critical. The writer sets the minister's mild phrase against residents wading through chest-deep water for four days. The contrast shows that the phrase understates the problem and that the writer does not accept the minister's view.

marking_scheme.step: Reason or evidence from the passage, in own words

questions.stem_md: An essay on road safety opens with two short sentences: thirty children cross a junction every day, and not one of them has a signal. Why might the writer begin like this instead of with a table of statistics?
questions.solution_md: Purpose: to engage the reader and make the problem concrete; link to the argument.

answer.model_answer_md: The two short sentences make the danger real and personal before any numbers appear. They hold the reader's attention at once and prepare the ground for the argument that the junction needs a signal.

marking_scheme.step: The point or inference that answers the question
Support from the passage, in own words

questions.stem_md: Read: *The villagers were reluctant to leave their homes, but the rising river left them no choice.* What does *reluctant* mean? Which clue in the sentence helped you?
questions.solution_md: Meaning: unwilling. Clue: contrast signalled by *but*.

answer.model_answer_md: Reluctant means unwilling or hesitant. The word but signals a contrast: the villagers did not want to leave, yet the rising river gave them no choice, so the contrast with leaving is the clue.

questions.stem_md: In 2022, 80 of the 200 Class 11 students of a school read a book for pleasure every week. In 2024, 90 of 250 did so (illustrative data). A headline says *Reading habit grows*. Is it fair? Use figures.
questions.solution_md: 80 of 200 is 40 per cent; 90 of 250 is 36 per cent.

answer.model_answer_md: Not entirely. The number of readers rose from 80 to 90, but the group grew from 200 to 250 students, so the share fell from 40 per cent to 36 per cent, a drop of 4 percentage points. The headline uses only the number.

marking_scheme.step: Compares shares: 40 per cent and 36 per cent
Judges the headline correctly, with reason

questions.stem_md: A passage on a school fair gives these points: stalls of handmade goods; money raised for the library; volunteers from Class 11; games for children; planning meetings in June; food stalls run by parents. Group them under two suitable headings.
questions.solution_md: Two headings that each name their group; every point placed under the right one.

answer.model_answer_md: Heading 1, Stalls and activities: handmade goods stalls, food stalls run by parents, games for children. Heading 2, Planning and purpose: planning meetings in June, volunteers from Class 11, money raised for the library.

questions.stem_md: Rewrite as one line of notes with at least two abbreviations, and give a key: *The government started a scheme in 2019 to give free books to students in rural areas.*
questions.solution_md: A short line with at least two abbreviations, all explained in the key.

answer.model_answer_md: Notes line: Govt. scheme (2019): free bks to rural stdts. Key: Govt. = government; bks = books; stdts = students. The line keeps the date, the giver, the benefit and the group, and drops the filler words.

marking_scheme.step: Short note line keeping all facts
Abbreviations used and explained in a key

questions.stem_md: Explain the difference between a heading and a sub-heading in notes, with one example.
questions.solution_md: Difference in level, plus an example.

answer.model_answer_md: A heading names a whole group of ideas, while a sub-heading names a smaller group inside it. For example, under the heading Advantages of cycling, the sub-headings could be Health and Cost, each with its own short points.

marking_scheme.step: Difference explained (whole group and smaller group)

questions.stem_md: Read: *The Class 8 recycling drive began in July with 12 volunteers. Each week they collected waste paper, which a local firm bought at a fixed rate. Mohan designed the poster, which was painted in blue. By December the drive had raised enough to buy 40 books for the library and had cut the school's paper waste by almost half.* Name two details to leave out of a 40-word summary and say why.
questions.solution_md: Two minor details named, with the reason that they are not main ideas.

answer.model_answer_md: Leave out Mohan's poster with its blue colour, and the number of volunteers at the start. They are small details which do not change the main idea: paper collected and sold funded library books and reduced waste.

questions.stem_md:
Read the passage and write a summary in about 50 words.

Every January, skies across many Indian cities fill with kites. The festival is joyful, but it has a darker side. Some flyers coat their thread with powdered glass to cut rivals' strings, and the sharp, strong thread injures birds that fly into it, and riders of two-wheelers who meet it at neck level. Hospitals report more injuries every season, and bird-rescue groups treat many wounded birds. Several states have banned glass-coated and synthetic thread, and volunteers now tie protective wires on motorbikes. Experts say the real remedy is a change of habit: plain cotton thread, flying from open rooftops away from roads, and never leaving broken thread in trees.
questions.solution_md: Main ideas: the harm done, the bans and protections, the safer habits. Drop the details of hospitals and rescue groups.

answer.model_answer_md: Kite festivals bring joy, but glass-coated and synthetic thread injures birds and road users. Some states have banned such thread and volunteers fit protective wires on bikes. Experts say safer habits, such as cotton thread, flying away from roads and clearing broken thread, are the real remedy.

marking_scheme.step: Main ideas: all key points of the passage covered, none of the examples copied
Brevity: about 50 words (40 to 60 accepted), no copying of whole sentences
Expression: own words, correct grammar and spelling, no personal opinion

questions.stem_md:
Read the passage and write a summary in about 50 words.

Many Indian cities were once dotted with lakes and tanks that stored monsoon rain and fed wells. As cities grew, builders filled many of them with soil to make land, and drains began to empty sewage into the rest. Without lakes, rain runs off the roads and floods low neighbourhoods, while groundwater falls because there is nothing to help the water soak into the ground. Some cities have started to restore their lakes, with citizens' groups removing weeds and councils stopping sewage from entering. Early results are encouraging, though experts warn that restoration will fail unless the land around a lake is also protected.
questions.solution_md: Main ideas: the old role of lakes, their loss and its effects, restoration, the warning.

answer.model_answer_md: Cities once had lakes that stored rain and fed wells, but many were filled for building or polluted by sewage, causing floods and falling groundwater. Citizens and councils are restoring some lakes, but experts warn this will fail unless the surrounding land is protected.

marking_scheme.step: Main ideas: all key points of the passage covered, none of the examples copied
Brevity: about 50 words (40 to 60 accepted), no copying of whole sentences
Expression: own words, correct grammar and spelling, no personal opinion

questions.stem_md:
A student wrote this 75-word draft as a summary of a notice about a colony's walking group. Rewrite it as a summary of about 50 words, keeping the main ideas.

Daily morning walks, which many doctors recommend, have become popular in our colony. Last month, about thirty residents, including Mr Rao, who is 72, began walking in the park at six. They say they sleep better, feel cheerful and have more energy through the day. The park, which has a jogging track and a small garden, has a new guard. Residents hope that more neighbours will join, and they plan to hold a health camp.
questions.solution_md: Keep who, what, the benefit and the plan; drop the age, the track and garden, and the new guard.

answer.model_answer_md: About thirty residents of the colony have begun walking in the park at six every morning. They say they sleep better and feel more cheerful and energetic. They hope more neighbours will join and plan to hold a health camp.

marking_scheme.step: Main ideas: all key points of the passage covered, none of the examples copied
Brevity: about 50 words (40 to 60 accepted), no copying of whole sentences
Expression: own words, correct grammar and spelling, no personal opinion

questions.stem_md:
Make notes on the passage in 50 to 80 words, with a title, headings and sub-headings, and abbreviations with a key.

India marks the turning points of its farming year with festivals. Pongal, in Tamil Nadu, falls in January, when rice is boiled in new pots until it overflows. Baisakhi, in Punjab, comes in April, when the wheat is ready for cutting, and farmers celebrate with fairs and folk dances. Bohag Bihu in Assam also comes in April and marks the Assamese new year and the start of sowing. Onam, in Kerala, is observed in late summer and early autumn, with flower carpets and a feast.
questions.solution_md: Group by season or by region; short points; key for TN and yr.

answer.model_answer_md:
Title: Farm Festivals of India

1. Winter and spring
   1.1 Pongal: TN, Jan; rice boiled in new pots till it overflows
   1.2 Baisakhi: Punjab, Apr; wheat ready; fairs, folk dances
   1.3 Bohag Bihu: Assam, Apr; new yr; sowing begins

2. Late summer
   2.1 Onam: Kerala, Aug-Sep; flower carpets, feast

Key: TN = Tamil Nadu; yr = year

marking_scheme.step: Two or more headings with sub-headings, logically grouped
All four festivals with state and time, in short points

questions.stem_md: A school magazine editorial says: *Our pass percentage rose from 82 to 91 after morning assemblies were shortened from 30 to 15 minutes. Shorter assemblies clearly produce better results, and every school should copy us.* Evaluate the strength of this argument in about 50 to 80 words.
questions.solution_md: 82 to 91 is a rise of 9 percentage points. Judgement: the evidence shows correlation only.

answer.model_answer_md: The argument is weak. It shows two events happening together, shorter assemblies and a nine-point rise in the pass percentage, but gives no evidence that one caused the other. Better teaching, easier papers or a different batch of students could explain the rise. One school's experience also cannot justify the claim that every school should copy it.

marking_scheme.step: Clear judgement: argument is weak or only partly convincing
Correlation is not shown to be cause; other explanations suggested
Comment on the sweeping generalisation, in own words

questions.stem_md: A library had 200 members in 2021 and lent 1,000 books; 250 members and 1,500 books in 2022; 300 members and 1,500 books in 2023 (illustrative data). A teacher says: *Borrowing has not grown since 2022, so members are losing interest.* Use figures to assess her claim in about 50 to 80 words.
questions.solution_md: Loans per member: 2021 is 5, 2022 is 6, 2023 is 5.

answer.model_answer_md: Total loans stayed at 1,500, but membership rose from 250 to 300, so loans per member fell from 6 to 5 (1,500 divided by 250 is 6; 1,500 divided by 300 is 5). The teacher is partly right: each member borrows less. But the library gained members, so interest is not simply being lost.

marking_scheme.step: Loans per member computed correctly for 2022 and 2023
Conclusion that each member borrows less
Balanced judgement using the rise in membership

questions.stem_md:
Make notes on the passage in 80 to 120 words, using a suitable title, headings and sub-headings, and abbreviations with a key.

A school roof is a large, free catchment for rain. On a roof of 800 square metres, a single heavy shower can send thousands of litres of water down the drains. Rainwater harvesting captures that water instead of wasting it. The simplest system has three parts: gutters along the roof edge, a pipe that carries the water down, and a filter before the water enters a storage tank or a recharge pit. Stored water can be used for gardening, cleaning and flushing toilets, which reduces the school's demand on the municipal supply. A recharge pit, on the other hand, lets the water soak into the ground and raises the water table over time.

Schools gain in other ways too. A working system is a live science lesson, since students can measure rainfall and calculate savings. It costs little to maintain if gutters are cleaned before every monsoon and the filter is checked each month. Schools that install such systems often report lower water bills.
questions.solution_md: Group the passage into why, parts, uses and other gains; keep points short; give a key.

answer.model_answer_md:
Title: Rainwater Harvesting in Schools

1. Why
   1.1 Roof = large free catchment
   1.2 800 sq m roof: thousands of litres lost in one shower
2. System parts
   2.1 Gutters
   2.2 Pipe
   2.3 Filter
   2.4 Tank or recharge pit
3. Uses
   3.1 Tank water: gardening, cleaning, toilets; less munic. supply
   3.2 Pit: raises water table
4. Other gains
   4.1 Live science lesson: measure rainfall, savings
   4.2 Low upkeep: clean gutters pre-monsoon; filter monthly
   4.3 Lower water bills

Key: sq m = square metres; munic. = municipal

marking_scheme.step: Title that sums up the passage
Headings and sub-headings that group the points logically, with numbering or indentation
Points complete, accurate and in short form (no full sentences)
Abbreviations used sensibly, with a key

questions.stem_md:
Make notes on the passage in 80 to 120 words, using a suitable title, headings and sub-headings, and abbreviations with a key.

Teenagers need between eight and ten hours of sleep each night, yet many get less. Part of the reason is biological: during adolescence the body clock shifts, so teenagers feel sleepy later in the evening and wake later in the morning. When school starts early, this natural rhythm collides with the timetable.

The effects of too little sleep are wide. Concentration and memory suffer, so students find it harder to learn and recall what they study. Mood drops too, and tired teenagers are more likely to feel irritable or anxious. Over time, poor sleep is linked with weaker immunity and a greater risk of accidents, especially for those who ride or drive.

Simple habits can help. Going to bed at a fixed time, keeping screens out of the bedroom, avoiding strong tea or coffee late in the day and getting daylight in the morning all improve sleep. Some schools have moved their start time later by thirty to sixty minutes and found that students were more alert and attended more regularly.
questions.solution_md: Three headings: need and causes, effects, remedies; short points; key.

answer.model_answer_md:
Title: Teenage Sleep: Need, Effects and Remedies

1. Need and causes
   1.1 8-10 hrs a night reqd; many get less
   1.2 Body clock shifts: sleepy late, wake late
   1.3 Early school clashes with this rhythm
2. Effects
   2.1 Poor concentration, memory
   2.2 Low mood: irritable, anxious
   2.3 Weak immunity; accident risk
3. Remedies
   3.1 Fixed bedtime
   3.2 No screens in bedroom
   3.3 No strong tea or coffee late
   3.4 Morning daylight
   3.5 Later school start (30-60 min): alert, regular attendance

Key: hrs = hours; reqd = required

marking_scheme.step: Title that sums up the passage
Headings and sub-headings that group the points logically, with numbering or indentation
Points complete, accurate and in short form (no full sentences)
Abbreviations used sensibly, with a key

questions.stem_md:
Read the passage. (a) Make notes on it with a title, headings and sub-headings and abbreviations with a key (3 marks). (b) Write a summary of it in about 40 words (2 marks). Use about 80 to 120 words in all.

Mangroves are salt-tolerant trees that grow along tropical coasts, where rivers meet the sea. The Sundarbans, shared by India and Bangladesh, is the largest mangrove forest in the world. Their tangled roots stand above the mud and hold the soil together, so the coastline erodes more slowly. In a storm, the dense roots and branches slow the waves and reduce the force of storm surges, protecting the villages behind them. Mangroves also act as nurseries: the sheltered, shallow water among the roots gives young fish and prawns a safe place to grow, which supports local fishing. In addition, mangroves store carbon in their roots and in the mud beneath them.

Yet mangroves are disappearing. They have been cleared for shrimp farms, ports and housing, and polluted by waste. Conservation groups now replant mangroves, and local communities are paid for protecting them, because restoring mangroves is cheaper than rebuilding sea walls after storms.
questions.solution_md: Notes: 3 marks (title, grouping, points, key). Summary: 2 marks (main ideas, brevity and own words).

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Notes
Title: Mangroves: Uses and Threats
1. Features
   1.1 Salt-tolerant trees; tropical coasts
   1.2 Sund. = largest mangrove forest
2. Benefits
   2.1 Roots hold soil: less erosion
   2.2 Slow waves, storm surges
   2.3 Fish and prawn nurseries: fishing
   2.4 Store carbon
3. Threats: cleared for shrimp farms, ports, housing; waste
4. Remedy: replanting; paid community protection
Key: Sund. = Sundarbans

(b) Summary
Mangroves steady coasts, shield villages from storms, shelter young fish and store carbon, but clearing and pollution are destroying them. Replanting, with communities paid to protect them, is cheaper than rebuilding sea walls.

questions.stem_md:
Below are a passage and a student's notes on it. (a) State three faults in the notes. (b) Rewrite the notes correctly. Use about 80 to 120 words in all.

**Passage.** India's postal network is the largest in the world by number of post offices, with offices in remote villages as well as cities. Besides letters and parcels, post offices offer savings accounts and small-savings schemes, and many sell insurance. In recent years the postal department has added digital services, such as tracking numbers for parcels and money transfer through mobile apps.

**Student's notes**
- India's postal network is the biggest in the whole world and it has offices in villages and cities
- Letters and parcels
- they also give savings accounts
- GPS: many services
- In recent years tracking no. for parcels
- Money transfer by apps; insurance sold
questions.solution_md: Three faults: sentences, no title or headings, unexplained abbreviation. Then a corrected, grouped version with a key.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Faults: the notes copy full sentences instead of short points; there is no title and no headings, so related points are scattered (insurance sits beside digital services); and GPS is an invented abbreviation, with no key.

(b) Title: India Post
1. Network: largest in world; offices in villages and cities
2. Services
   2.1 Letters, parcels
   2.2 Savings a/cs, small-savings schemes
   2.3 Insurance
3. Digital
   3.1 Parcel tracking nos.
   3.2 Money transfer: mobile apps
Key: a/cs = accounts; nos. = numbers

marking_scheme.step: Rewritten with title and logical headings
Short points, accurate, no loss of facts

questions.stem_md:
Read the passage and the two student summaries. (a) Say what is wrong with each summary. (b) Write your own summary in about 40 words. Use about 80 to 120 words in all.

**Passage.** Community radio stations are small, low-power broadcasters run by and for a local community. They are usually heard within a radius of about fifteen kilometres and broadcast in the local language. Programmes cover farming advice, weather warnings, health messages and folk songs recorded by villagers. Unlike commercial stations they are not run for profit, and volunteers from the area often present shows. In coastal villages such stations have broadcast cyclone warnings in time for fishermen to return. Their greatest strength is trust: listeners hear familiar voices speaking about familiar problems.

**Summary A.** Community radio stations are small, low-power broadcasters run by and for a local community, and they are usually heard within a radius of about fifteen kilometres and they broadcast in the local language and programmes cover farming advice, weather warnings, health messages and folk songs.

**Summary B.** Community radio is a wonderful idea that every village should have. It serves farmers, warns of cyclones and is run by volunteers in the local language.
questions.solution_md: A: copied, too long, incomplete. B: opinion, misses trust. Own summary in fresh words, with the main ideas.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Summary A copies the passage word for word, is too long and stops before the cyclone warnings and the point about trust. Summary B is short, but it begins with the summary-writer's own opinion, which does not belong in a summary, and it leaves out the idea of trust.

(b) Community radio stations are non-profit, volunteer-run broadcasters serving a small area in the local language. They carry farming advice, weather and health messages, and have even given cyclone warnings. Their strength is trust, as listeners hear familiar voices discussing familiar problems.

marking_scheme.step: Fault in Summary A: copied, too long and incomplete
Fault in Summary B: opinion and an omitted main idea
Own summary covers purpose, content and trust
Own summary in about 40 words, in own words

questions.stem_md:
Read the extract from a principal's annual message, then evaluate his argument in 80 to 120 words: say what is convincing, what is weak and what further evidence you would want.

*Since phones became common among our students three years ago, our average in the half-yearly examination has fallen from 71 to 64 per cent. Students use phones to chat in class, and they sleep late scrolling. A complete ban on phones on campus is the only sensible response. Parents who disagree are putting convenience before their children's future.*
questions.solution_md: A judgement with both sides: seven-point fall and possible distraction; weaknesses: correlation, no comparison, personal attack; further evidence.

answer.model_answer_md: The argument has some force: the average has fallen by seven percentage points, and phones can distract in class and cut sleep. As proof, however, it is weak. The fall followed phones, but harder papers or changes of teacher could also explain it, and the principal compares no phone users with non-users. The remark about disagreeing parents attacks people instead of answering their view. I would want results by phone use, figures from other years and a trial of limited rules, such as phones kept in bags during lessons, before accepting a total ban.

marking_scheme.step: What is convincing: the fall and the plausible effects
Weaknesses: cause not proved; no comparison group
The unfair remark about parents identified
Further evidence or a reasoned alternative
